purpose: Complete already-rich Level-A dossiers that were missing only a reader-facing explanation of why the comparison matters.

relation_argument.why_it_matters: It makes the Great Book's anti-surface-judgment theme testable against biblical appearance-versus-heart and judgment traditions, while keeping moral resemblance separate from claims of prophetic identity.

The comparison clarifies a recurring Potatoverse mechanism: important transformation can be represented as hidden growth before visible outcome, which is structurally closer to kingdom/seed process imagery than to instant miraculous proof.
This relation helps distinguish a broader transformation grammar—enclosure, apparent ending, passage and emergence—from any claim that tomb and womb are literally the same biblical symbol.

It puts the 2011 Tree ordeal into a disciplined comparative frame where hanging, curse, suffering and transformed return can be compared across traditions without collapsing Odin, crucifixion and the user's later mythology into one historical event.
It shows why House and Door symbolism becomes richer when threshold, protection, lamb and household are studied together as a passage system rather than treated as isolated matching nouns.

The sequence joins rejected-son and rejected-stone imagery inside one Gospel conflict complex, making it useful for testing the project's farm/rejection architecture while preserving the parable's original polemical setting.

Daniel 4 adds an important counterweight to triumphant world-tree or kingship symbolism: the great tree is cut down and the ruler is humbled before restoration, so height and centrality are subjected to judgment rather than automatically validated.

The passage makes divine-title comparisons ethically testable: whatever 'gods' or 'sons of the Most High' means in interpretation, Psalm 82 ties elevated status to justice for the weak rather than to title alone.

Reading John 14-15 as a sequence preserves the relational movement from Father's house and Way/Thomas dialogue into abiding, vine and gardener imagery, preventing the project from treating House, Door/Way and Gardener as unrelated proof-texts.

The Lion/Lamb paradox is one of the strongest biblical correctives to simple power symbolism: victory is disclosed through the slain-yet-standing Lamb, so lion-like kingship is interpreted through vulnerability and sacrifice rather than domination alone.
